title: La Bàn - Career Guidance for Vietnamese AI Transition webmcp
pitch: La Bàn turns a career-guidance website into an in-browser MCP server: the AI agent a Vietnamese worker already trusts reads our verified occupation database and research library...
about_excerpt: La Bàn turns a career-guidance website into an in-browser MCP server: the AI agent a Vietnamese worker already trusts reads our verified occupation database and research library... Like 1 Comment Story Updates A screen demo of chatGpt in-app Note: the app is hosted on Render's free tier, so the server spins down after 15 minutes of inactivity - the first request may take up to a minute while it wakes up. Once warm, everything responds quickly. Inspiration The ILO estimates generative AI could impact more than 20% of jobs in Vietnam — and nearly 80 million workers across ASEAN are in occupations likely to be affected. Millions of them are asking the same question: "Will AI take my job - and what should I learn?" The answers they get online are generic, and when LLMs write them, the citations are sometimes fabricated. We measured it: across 12 Vietnamese worker personas, a single-prompt baseline produced 2 fabricated citations out of 26 - fluent, confident, and unverifiable. For decisions this life-altering, that's disqualifying. La Bàn (Vietnamese for The Compass ) already existed as a career-guidance platform with a curated Vietnam occupation database and research library. The WebMCP Challenge gave us the missing piece: instead of being a destination the worker visits once, the site could become the evidence engine behind every agent conversation about their career. Existing tools are either static career sites (no agent) or chatbots (no verifiable data, no persistence, no human gate) — La Bàn brings the three together: the page supplies the evidence, the agent reasons over it, and the human holds the pen. What it does La Bàn is an in-browser MCP server . Open it in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) and your agent immediately gets 12 tools in three layers: Evidence (client-side, works with zero API keys): lookup_occupation reads a curated Vietnam resilience database with MOLISA/O*NET codes and task-level automation exposure; search_research returns verifiable sources from WEF, ILO, the World Bank and more. Analysis : analyze_career_transition runs a verified multi-agent pipeline (Profiler → Evidence Gatherer → Analyst → Verifier) where only what the tools return can be cited , and every citation is checked against the corpus. Workspace (writes): save_career_plan , add_milestone , update_milestone_progress , share_plan_to_community - every single write opens an approval modal inside the page . A rejection means the agent asks what to change; it never retries blindly. The human and the agent share one page. What used to be tab-switching between a chatbot and a static website — with nothing saved or tracked — becomes a single conversation: the agent looks up the occupation, pulls the research, scores the risk, and drafts an editable 90-day plan; the human edits it in a modal before it's saved, both track progress across sessions, and an Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call in real time. Writes never happen without explicit human approval. How we built it Progressive enhancement : tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool with JSON Schema inputs and readOnlyHint annotations. In a normal browser the app runs unchanged; in an agent's browser it becomes a workspace. The honesty layer : when an occupation isn't in the database (a watch repairer, for example), lookup_occupation says so - and the agent falls back to research evidence instead of inventing a resilience score. Verification-first pipeline : the Verifier checks schema, guardrails and every citation; on failure, the analyst repairs its own output. Ablation showed the interesting part: tools alone changed nothing on grounding - the verifier loop is what eliminated fabrication (91.7% → 100% grounding, 2 → 0 hallucinated citations, 12/12 valid schemas). Stack : React 19 + Express + Gemini (multi-agent pipeline), localStorage workspace persistence, deployed on Render's free tier. 119 unit tests cover the agents, verification and every WebMCP handler. Challenges we ran into requestUserInteraction is not universally supported. During rehearsal on the real ChatGPT in-app browser, the Codex WebMCP shim exposed the API but threw on every call, breaking all workspace writes. The fix: treat the wrapper as best-effort with a try/catch fallback to the in-page modal - the human gate stays intact in every runtime. Free-tier reality. Our analysis endpoint was "timing out" in ChatGPT - but measured directly it returns a full verified result in ~16 seconds warm. The real culprit was Render's spin-down after 15 idle minutes. Cold start, not code. Teaching an agent to say "I don't know." The database covers 10 occupations. Designing tools whose no-match response is genuinely useful - and watching ChatGPT relay that honesty instead of hallucinating - was the most satisfying moment of the project. Accomplishments & what we learned A baseline with measurable fabrication became a demo where the agent refuses to invent data in front of a live audience. Writing WebMCP tools is really API design for a new kind of user - the tool descriptions we wrote read like prompts, and the agent followed them ("call this FIRST", "cite these instead of guessing"). Retrieval alone doesn't stop fabrication. Verification that can send work back does. Try it: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask "I'm an accountant in Hanoi, will AI replace me?" - then say "Save me a 90-day plan to become a data analyst" and approve it in the page.
